1.note: The psalmist is using the term **name** to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [call on him]

3.note: Here, **the name of his holiness** represents Yahweh himself, who is holy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in Yahweh, who is holy]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **name** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in his holy name]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts, feelings, and desires exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let the people who seek Yahweh rejoice]

The psalmist is speaking of people who desire to know Yahweh as if they were **seekers** of him, or trying to find him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let the heart of those who desire to know Yahweh rejoice]

4.note: The psalmist is speaking of needing to **Seek Yahweh** as if he were a lost object that needed to be sought and found. He means that the people should pray to Yahweh and desire to be in his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pray to Yahweh and ask for his strength]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for him to strengthen you]
Here, **his face** represents his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [seek his presence]

5.note: Here, **his mouth** represents Yahweh speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the decrees that he spoke]

6.q: זֶ֭רַע אַבְרָהָ֣ם עַבְדּ֑⁠וֹ בְּנֵ֖י יַעֲקֹ֣ב בְּחִירָֽי⁠ו
6.note: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could move 105:6 before 105:7 as the UST does, in order to state who is being addressed before giving the content of the speech. You would then combine the verses into a verse bridge (105:5–6).

The psalmist is speaking of the Israelites as if they were the **seed of Abraham**. He means that they are Abraham’s descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [descendants of Abraham]
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s servant]

The psalmist is speaking as if the people of Israel were the **sons** of Jacob. He means that they are his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [descendants of Jacob]

The psalmist is using the adjective **chosen** as a noun to mean people who are chosen. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you could translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those he has chosen]

7.note: By using this possessive form, our God, the psalmist is not saying that the Israelites possess or control Yahweh. Rather he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship as modeled in the UST.

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s decrees as if they were physical objects that existed **in all the earth**. He means that Yahweh’s laws and judgments apply to all people everywhere on earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His laws apply to everyone on earth]

8.note: The psalmist assumes that his audience will understand that God’s remembering is not merely recalling information but actively maintaining and fulfilling his commitments. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He keeps in mind]

8.q: זָכַ֣ר לְ⁠עוֹלָ֣ם בְּרִית֑⁠וֹ דָּבָ֥ר צִ֝וָּ֗ה לְ⁠אֶ֣לֶף דּֽוֹר
8.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [He remembers his covenant forever, yes, the word he commanded for a thousand generations]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he remembers the word he commanded]

Here, **the word** represents the covenant that God spoke. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the covenant he commanded]

The psalmist is using **for a thousand generations** as a common expression of his culture to mean “for all time” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for all time]

9.note: The psalmist is using the phrase **he cut** as a common expression of his culture to mean “he made.” This idiom comes from the ancient practice of cutting animals in two as part of making a covenant. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that he made]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the covenant that he cut]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the sentence if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he remembers his oath]

10.q: וַ⁠יַּֽעֲמִידֶ֣⁠הָ לְ⁠יַעֲקֹ֣ב לְ⁠חֹ֑ק לְ֝⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל בְּרִ֣ית עוֹלָֽם
10.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [He confirmed it to Jacob as a statute; yes, to Israel, an everlasting covenant]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the sentence if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he confirmed it to Israel, an everlasting covenant]

11.note: This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a first-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a direct quotation.
Here **your** is plural, indicating that Yahweh made this same covenant with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their descendants. Use the plural form here if your language marks that distinction.

12.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]
The pronoun **it** refers to the land of Canaan. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the land of Canaan]

13.note: These two phrases **from nation to nation** and **from a kingdom to other people** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [repeatedly from one kingdom to another]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **kingdom**. He means kingdoms in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from one kingdom]

14.note: The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [because of the people of Israel] or [for the sake of the people of Israel]

15.note: This is the beginning of what God said to the kings. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a first-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a direct quotation.

The psalmist says **Do not touch** as a warning against doing even the slightest harm to emphasize God’s strictness about this. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [In no way should you hurt]

16.note: The psalmist is speaking of the famine as if it were something that could hear and respond to Yahweh **calling** it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He made the land produce a famine]

The psalmist is using **he broke all of the staff of bread** as a common expression of his culture to mean “he caused there to be a famine” or “he made it so that there was no food.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he made the land unable to produce food]
The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [food]

17.note: The pronoun **He** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh sent]
The pronoun **them** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that God orchestrated Joseph’s sale into slavery as part of his plan to send Joseph ahead to Egypt. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Joseph was the man whom Yahweh sent ahead by allowing him to be sold as a servant]

18.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the prison guards in Egypt. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The prison guards in Egypt oppressed]

A **shackle** is a device made of metal used to restrain a prisoner by fastening around the ankles or wrists. If your readers would not be familiar with what a shackle is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [in metal restraints used to fasten a prisoner’s wrists or ankles together]

By **the iron**, the psalmist means an iron collar that was put around Joseph’s neck. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [an iron collar attached to a chain]

19.note: Here, **his word** represents what Joseph said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the things that he said]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s testing of Joseph as if Yahweh were a metalworker who **refined** him. This image pictures God’s word purifying and strengthening Joseph’s character during his time of suffering, just as fire removes impurities from metal. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [tested and taught him]

20.q: שָׁ֣לַח מֶ֭לֶךְ וַ⁠יַּתִּירֵ֑⁠הוּ מֹשֵׁ֥ל עַ֝מִּ֗ים וַֽ⁠יְפַתְּחֵֽ⁠הוּ

If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [The king sent and released him; yes, the one ruling the people, and liberated him]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The king sent officials and released him]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the one ruling the people sent officials]

21.note: The pronoun **He** refers to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, while the pronoun **him** refers to Joseph. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The king appointed Joseph]

Here, **house** represents everything concerning the king’s palace. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of everything concerning his palace]

22.note: The psalmist is speaking of the officials of Egypt as if they were **his princes**. The psalmist means that Pharaoh gave Joseph authority over Egypt’s highest-ranking officials. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his chief rulers]

The psalmist is using **according to his soul** as a common expression of his culture to mean “according to his will” or “according to his desire.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to subject his princes to Joseph’s desires]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He appointed him to bind his princes according to his soul]

23.q: וַ⁠יָּבֹ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל מִצְרָ֑יִם וְ֝⁠יַעֲקֹ֗ב גָּ֣ר בְּ⁠אֶֽרֶץ־חָֽם
23.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Alternate translation: [Then Israel came into Egypt; yes, Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham]

24.note: The pronoun **He** refers to Yahweh. The pronoun **his** refers to Jacob. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh made Jacob’s people very fruitful]

The psalmist is speaking of God causing his people to increase in number as if he were making them **fruitful**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He made his people multiply greatly]

The pronouns **him** and **his** refer to **people**, which is singular in form. If it would be helpful, you could use plural pronouns instead. Alternate translation: [and he made them stronger than their enemies]

25.note: The psalmist is speaking of God changing the Egyptians’ attitudes as if he had physically **turned their hearts**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He changed their emotions]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He turned their hearts to plot against his servants]

26.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [He sent Aaron]

The expression **whom he had chosen him** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in many languages, since the word **whom** already indicates Aaron as the object. If it would be clearer in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [whom he had chosen]

27.q: שָֽׂמוּ־בָ֭⁠ם דִּבְרֵ֣י אֹתוֹתָ֑י⁠ו וּ֝⁠מֹפְתִ֗ים בְּ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ חָֽם

Here, **his words** represents what God said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he said to them]

33.note: The psalmist assumes that readers will know that God struck the vines and fig trees with the hail mentioned in the previous verse. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He destroyed]

45.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [they might keep his statutes, that is, comply with his laws]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]
